context: site network · fire pumps & tank are long-lead; ring main in service before fuel or occupancy

brief.intro: New to this project type? A fire water network is the buried ring of pressure pipe that feeds hydrants, monitors and the sprinkler and deluge systems of a plant, a compound or a district. A dedicated tank and a set of fire pumps (usually electric and diesel, plus a small jockey pump that keeps the ring pressurised) stand behind it. The pipe laying is ordinary underground pipe work; what makes the job special is that it is a life-safety system. It must be built to the fire code, witnessed and accepted by the civil defence authority or the insurer, and it must be in service before fuel, hydrocarbons or people arrive — so its completion date is fixed by other milestones, not by its own length.

scope.name: Fire water storage tank
scope.desc: Dedicated tank sized for the required flow and duration.

scope.name: Fire pump house
scope.desc: Electric, diesel and jockey pumps with controllers, fuel tank and test line.

scope.name: Ring main
scope.desc: Buried HDPE / DI / GRE main looped around the protected area.

scope.name: Sectional isolation valves
scope.desc: Post-indicator valves that let a damaged section be isolated while the rest stays live.

scope.name: Hydrants & monitors
scope.desc: Pillar hydrants, hose cabinets and fixed monitors at the required spacing.

scope.name: Branch connections
scope.desc: Feeds to building sprinkler risers, deluge skids and foam systems.

scope.name: Thrust restraint
scope.desc: Thrust blocks or restrained joints at every change of direction.

scope.name: Power, control & alarms
scope.desc: Pump power supplies, controllers and signals to the fire alarm panel.

scope.name: Flushing & pressure testing
scope.desc: High-velocity flushing and a hydrostatic test, witnessed.

scope.name: Pump acceptance & authority approval
scope.desc: Pump performance test, flow test at the hydrants and the authority inspection.

glossary.plain: a looped main, so any hydrant can be fed from two directions.
a small pump that keeps the ring at pressure and covers small leaks, so the main pumps do not start needlessly.
the pump that still runs when the power fails; it has its own fuel tank and batteries.
a buried isolation valve with a post above ground showing OPEN or SHUT.
a fixed water cannon for cooling or fighting a fire from a distance.
open nozzles that drench a piece of equipment when a valve opens.
holding the main at a set test pressure for a set time to prove it is tight.
running water through the main at high velocity to remove debris before it is connected to sprinklers.
running each fire pump at no flow, rated flow and 150 % flow to prove its performance curve.

must_get_right: Find the date when fuel, hydrocarbons or occupants first arrive, and set fire-water 'in service' before it as a contract milestone — then plan backwards.
Order the fire pumps, controllers and diesel engine at the start: they are listed / approved equipment with long delivery, and they need a finished pump house.
Flush before connecting the building and deluge systems, and test before backfilling the joints where the code requires them exposed.
Book the authority or insurer witness for the pressure test and the pump acceptance test; their availability is part of the schedule.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by ring section (between sectional valves) with the tank and pump house as a separate branch, so partial rings can be put in service area by area.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar. Witnessed tests are fixed-date activities agreed with the authority or insurer.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Two chains meet at commissioning: (1) trench → ring main → thrust blocks cured → flushing → hydrostatic test → backfill; (2) tank and pump house → pumps and controllers → power → pump acceptance test. Authority acceptance needs both, and must precede the first fuel / hydrocarbon / occupancy milestone.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The fire-protection design is approved by the authority before procurement; permanent or approved temporary power is available for the pump test; water is available to fill the tank and flush.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Listed fire pumps, diesel engine & controllers
Fire water tank (bolted steel / GRP panels)
Before the ring main is closed for testing

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: The ring shares corridors with other buried services and must be coordinated with roads and foundations. Listed equipment cannot be substituted without re-approval.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late approval of the design, late fire pumps, a failed pressure test under completed paving, and authority comments at the final inspection. Contingency is held before the in-service milestone.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by ring section and system; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the pipe-laying and pump-installation crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
